name: radix-heap (pair_radix_heap)
workload: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on real USA road networks (264K to 24M vertices, DIMACS challenge-9 datasets), averaged over 100 random sources; measures both pure priority-queue time and overall algorithm time
claimed_speedup: up to ~1.7x faster on the pure priority-queue workload (e.g. USA.gr: rheap 1.222667s vs stl 2.119727s) and ~1.25-1.29x faster on overall Dijkstra time including edge traversal (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: radix heap is a monotone priority queue: popped keys must be non-decreasing, so it only supports algorithms like Dijkstra with non-negative edge weights, not general priority-queue use; not a drop-in std::priority_queue replacement
caveats: Benchmark dates to 2015 on hardware/compiler of that era; no LICENSE file in repo so code is reference-only, not confirmed redistributable; repo has had no commits since 2015
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "radix heap" (variation on seed query "heap faster than std::priority_queue benchmark")

name: prio_queue (rollbear)
workload: 320 push + 320 pop cycles of random values at increasing queue sizes, comparing a cache-friendly B-heap layout (mini-heap sizes 8/16/32/64) against std::priority_queue<int> and std::priority_queue<pair<int,int>>
claimed_speedup: "always faster than std::priority_queue<int>" across all tested mini-heap sizes, and "consistently much faster than std::priority_queue<std::pair<int,int>>" when priority and payload are stored in separate arrays; exact ratios are shown only in the post's benchmark graphs, not stated as numeric text
hardware: Intel Core i7-4500U, 32KB L1d cache, 64-byte cache lines
tradeoffs: best performance requires storing priority and payload in separate arrays rather than a combined pair/struct; mini-heap size must be tuned to the cache line size; the same blog post reports worse performance than std::priority_queue for a std::pair<int, unique_ptr<msg>> payload in some configurations; less battle-tested than std::priority_queue
caveats: Benchmark methodology (CPU, compiler, flags) is fully stated but is from 2015 on now-old hardware; no absolute timings or numeric multipliers are given in the post's text, only relative graphs; repo's last commit (2025-09-18) is just over 12 months before this run
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "pairing heap OR 4-ary heap C++ github benchmark faster than std::priority_queue" -> rollbear/prio_queue README linking to benchmark blog post
